name: Ethnographic Synthesis
title: Ethnographic Synthesis
answer: Ethnographic synthesis is the practice of combining findings from multiple ethnographic or qualitative field studies into a single comparative account. It sits within qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where the aim is to preserve the texture of local context while drawing out patterns that hold across sites. Unlike a simple literature review, it treats each study as a case with its own setting, participants and history, and it asks what can legitimately be said across those cases. The unit of synthesis is usually the theme, the practice or the account rather than the individual participant.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Ethnographic synthesis is the practice of combining findings from multiple ethnographic or qualitative field studies into a single comparative account. It sits within qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where the aim is to preserve the texture of local context while drawing out patterns that hold across sites. Unlike a simple literature review, it treats each study as a case with its own setting, participants and history, and it asks what can legitimately be said across those cases. The unit of synthesis is usually the theme, the practice or the account rather than the individual participant.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of qualitative data analysis software, reference managers and shared coding frameworks. Common tools include NVivo, ATLAS.ti, Dedoose and MAXQDA for coding and memoing, alongside spreadsheets or databases for tracking themes across studies. Teams often maintain a shared codebook, a matrix of cases by themes, and a document trail linking every synthesised claim back to the source study. Where the corpus is large, retrieval and screening may be supported by search tools, but the interpretive work stays with the analysts.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical sequence is to define a review question, assemble a purposive set of studies, appraise them for relevance and quality, then extract context and findings into a common frame. Analysts code the extracted material, build themes, and compare them across cases, often using matrices or network displays to see where accounts converge and where they conflict. Reflexivity matters throughout, since the synthesis team's own assumptions shape what gets coded and how themes are named. Reporting usually includes a methods account, a findings narrative and a clear statement of how each claim traces back to its source studies.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on consent, confidentiality and the provenance of quoted material. Participants in the original studies consented to a particular use, and secondary synthesis can stretch that consent, so anonymisation and re-identification risk need active management. Reviewers should record how each study was found, why it was included or excluded, and how each synthesised claim maps to its sources, so that readers can audit the chain. Where the site reports on this work it links to the original paper rather than to a search tool, which keeps the provenance visible. Ethical review, data sharing agreements and funder or journal policies all shape what can be published.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more transparent and more cumulative synthesis, with living reviews that are updated as new studies appear and with shared reporting standards for qualitative evidence. Machine assistance is entering at the screening and coding stages, which raises questions about how much interpretation can be delegated and how that delegation is documented. There is growing interest in combining ethnographic synthesis with quantitative evidence in mixed methods designs, and in making the underlying data and codebooks reusable. The persistent tension is between scale and depth, since larger corpora invite automation while the method's value rests on close attention to context.
